pittance

PIT-uhns · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Pittance is a very small or unfairly small amount of money.

The playwright spent his final years surviving on little more than a pittance from occasional royalty checks.

Example

The internship promised valuable experience, but the pay itself was a pittance, barely enough for a single week of groceries.

An amount of money so small it feels almost insulting, especially compared to what the work or effort deserved, is exactly what a pittance is.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

paltry sum: A paltry sum is an amount of money so small it is disappointing or even contemptible, in any context at all. A pittance is more pointed: it is what someone is paid or given to live on, insultingly little next to the effort, need, or value behind it.

meager wage: A meager wage is ongoing pay that is barely enough to live on — the word measures the wage against the cost of living, week after week. A pittance measures the amount against what was deserved: pay or reward so small it lands as an insult.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

fortune: a very large amount of money

windfall: a large amount of money received unexpectedly

Where it sits · how insultingly small the amount

modest sum → pittance → starvation wage

modest sum vs. pittance: A modest sum is weaker than a pittance: a modest sum is simply small or unimpressive, while a pittance is smaller and stingier, insultingly little for what it should cover.

starvation wage vs. pittance: A starvation wage is more extreme than a pittance: a pittance is insultingly small pay, but a starvation wage goes further, too little even to keep a worker fed.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — piet- (pietas): piety, dutifulness (Latin, via Old French pitance)

Put it together: Pittance traces back through Old French pitance, a small allowance of food once given to monks out of piety, to Latin pietas, 'piety.' A pittance was originally a tiny, charitable ration; today the word describes any payment that's almost insultingly small.

Use the root in a new word: piety: The monastery's daily rituals reflected centuries of quiet piety.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Pittance almost always implies unfairness -- the amount is too small compared to the effort, need, or value involved. It connects naturally to indigent (later in this unit): a person paid a pittance for long enough can easily become indigent.
